words.shortDefinition: Server-Side Request Forgery; server fetches an attacker-supplied URL, using its own credentials and network position.
words.simpleDefinition: SSRF tricks a server into making HTTP requests on behalf of an attacker. The server — not the attacker's browser — sends the request, so it carries the server's IP address, IAM credentials, and access to internal services. Webhooks, image-import URLs, and PDF generators that fetch remote assets are the most common entry points.
words.longDefinition: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) occurs wherever a web application accepts a user-supplied URL and fetches it server-side without adequate controls. The attack surface includes webhook endpoints, URL-import features, document converters, translation proxies, and URL-preview generators. The threat model rests on three asymmetries: network position (the server may be inside a VPC that blocks direct attacker access), implicit trust (cloud metadata endpoints and internal APIs accept requests from the application tier without authentication), and credential exposure (responses may carry IAM tokens, API keys, or internal service secrets). The canonical real-world case is the Capital One 2019 breach, in which a misconfigured WAF with an overprivileged IAM role was exploited via SSRF against the AWS IMDSv1 endpoint at 169.254.169.254, resulting in the exfiltration of over 100 million credit application records. SSRF was added as OWASP A10:2021, elevated from an obscure footnote to a standalone category precisely because cloud deployments made the internal metadata endpoint a near-universal high-value target.
words.connector: Think of SSRF like a drive-through proxy: you order through the speaker, but the food ends up in your car. You tell the server where to go, it goes there using its own keycard and returns whatever it finds — internal APIs, cloud credentials, private network scans.
words.techContext: An attacker submitting `{"url": "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ec2-role"}` to a webhook endpoint may receive temporary AWS credentials if the server is running on EC2 without IMDSv2 enforcement.
words.exampleSentence: After discovering SSRF in the invoice-upload feature, the researcher pivoted to the internal Kubernetes API server and retrieved service-account tokens in under ten minutes.

codeExample.code:
import ipaddress, socket, urllib.parse

BLOCKED = [
    ipaddress.ip_network("169.254.0.0/16"),  # IMDS
    ipaddress.ip_network("10.0.0.0/8"),
    ipaddress.ip_network("172.16.0.0/12"),
    ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.0.0/16"),
    ipaddress.ip_network("127.0.0.0/8"),
]

def is_safe_url(url: str) -> bool:
    p = urllib.parse.urlparse(url)
    if p.scheme not in ("http", "https"):
        return False  # block file://, gopher://, dict://
    resolved = socket.getaddrinfo(p.hostname, None)[0][4][0]
    ip = ipaddress.ip_address(resolved)
    return not any(ip in net for net in BLOCKED)

words.etymology: Coined in a 2012 blog post by security researcher Jerry Hicks and popularized by PortSwigger and SSRF-research papers through the mid-2010s; the cloud metadata angle elevated it to mainstream awareness around 2019.

words.shortDefinition: SSRF variant where the response is not returned to the attacker; detection relies on out-of-band DNS or timing signals.
words.simpleDefinition: In blind SSRF the server makes your request but never shows you the response. You prove it happened by watching your own DNS resolver or HTTP listener for a callback from the server's IP. Even without a visible response, blind SSRF can pivot to internal services that accept commands rather than only returning data.
words.longDefinition: Blind SSRF arises when the application fetches an attacker-controlled URL but discards or never surfaces the response body — a webhook checker, SEO crawler, or SSL certificate verifier may return only a status code. Detection techniques include: out-of-band DNS callbacks (submitting a URL pointing to an attacker-controlled subdomain such as via Burp Collaborator or interactsh, then watching DNS logs for a lookup from the server's IP), HTTP callbacks (running a listener that logs incoming requests and their source IPs), time-based inference (internal hosts respond quickly; non-existent hosts time out — measurable even without a response body), and error-message leakage (applications that return different errors for unreachable vs refused connections expose network topology). Exploitation chains for blind SSRF include gopher:// protocol tricks to speak raw TCP to internal Redis, Memcached, or SMTP servers; pivoting to internal admin APIs that accept command parameters; and abusing Kubernetes API servers that trust pod-network traffic without mTLS.
words.connector: Blind SSRF is like hiring a courier to deliver a note to a locked building and timing how quickly they return — you never see what happened inside, but the return time and any callback tell you whether someone was home.
words.techContext: A bug bounty researcher confirming blind SSRF typically registers a unique Burp Collaborator domain, submits it as the webhook URL, and waits for the DNS interaction log to show a lookup from the target server's outbound IP.
words.exampleSentence: The security researcher confirmed blind SSRF by submitting a Collaborator URL to the PDF export endpoint and observing a DNS lookup arrive from the application server's egress IP within two seconds.

codeExample.code:
# Detect blind SSRF with an out-of-band HTTP callback server
from http.server import HTTPServer, BaseHTTPRequestHandler

class CallbackHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        print(f"[SSRF callback] From: {self.client_address[0]}")
        print(f"[SSRF callback] Path: {self.path}")
        self.send_response(200)
        self.end_headers()

# Submit http://<your-server>/ssrf-test as the webhook URL
# If the app fetches it, this server logs the server's outbound IP
HTTPServer(('0.0.0.0', 8080), CallbackHandler).serve_forever()

words.etymology: "Blind" borrowed from blind SQL injection — the attacker cannot see the result directly and must use side-channel techniques to confirm the vulnerability; the SSRF-specific usage became standard terminology around 2016.

words.shortDefinition: Broken Object-Level Authorization (OWASP API #1); API returns any object by ID without checking caller ownership.
words.simpleDefinition: BOLA is the API-first renaming of IDOR. An endpoint accepts an object ID, looks it up, and returns it — without verifying that the requesting user owns or is authorized to access that object. Changing an order ID in the URL from your own to another user's yields that user's data. BOLA has ranked as the single most critical API security risk since the OWASP API Top 10 was introduced in 2019.
words.longDefinition: Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA), defined as OWASP API1:2023, is the most widespread and highest-impact category in the API security landscape. The root cause is a missing or bypassed authorization check at the resource-retrieval layer: the application authenticates the caller (knows who they are) but fails to authorize the access (does not verify they are allowed to access that specific object). APIs are particularly susceptible because they expose internal identifiers — database row IDs, UUIDs, account numbers — that clients must supply in every request. Sequential integer IDs make enumeration trivial; even UUIDs can be harvested from other legitimate API responses and replayed. BOLA manifests in GET (data leakage), PUT/PATCH (unauthorized modification), and DELETE (unauthorized deletion) operations. In financial APIs, BOLA on account endpoints has led to full exfiltration of transaction histories across entire user bases. The defense requires enforcing ownership checks server-side on every object retrieval: verify that the authenticated principal is the owner of or has been explicitly granted access to the requested object.
words.connector: BOLA is the equivalent of a hotel that gives you a room key and then lets you open any room if you just ask for its number — the lock exists, but asking for a different room number bypasses it entirely.
words.techContext: A BOLA finding in a bug bounty report typically shows two cURL commands: one authenticated as user A fetching `/api/orders/10482`, and one authenticated as user B fetching the same URL — both returning data belonging to user A.
words.exampleSentence: The BOLA vulnerability in the fintech API allowed any authenticated user to retrieve another customer's full transaction history by incrementing the account_id path parameter.
words.etymology: BOLA is the OWASP API Security Top 10 term (introduced 2019) for what the OWASP Web Application Top 10 has called IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) since 2007; the rename reflects an API-first framing.

words.shortDefinition: Broken Function-Level Authorization; user calls admin or privileged API endpoints not intended for their role.
words.simpleDefinition: BFLA is what happens when admin-only API endpoints are accessible by ordinary authenticated users — because the code checks authentication but not role. The admin `/delete-user` button is hidden in the UI, but any authenticated user who discovers and calls the URL directly succeeds. BFLA is OWASP API5:2023.
words.longDefinition: Broken Function-Level Authorization (BOLA addresses the data dimension; BFLA addresses the function dimension) occurs when higher-privilege operations — administrative endpoints, billing actions, bulk data exports — are accessible to lower-privilege callers. The canonical failure pattern: an application has separate URL paths for user and admin operations (`/api/v1/users` vs `/api/v1/admin/users`), but the authorization check confirms only that the request carries a valid token, not that the token belongs to an admin-tier principal. BFLA is widespread in mobile app backends, where admin functions are assumed to be hidden because the UI does not expose them, and in internal tooling promoted to public APIs where the original network-level trust has been removed. Three sub-patterns are particularly common: HTTP method confusion (GET has a role check, DELETE does not), URL manipulation (guessing admin-prefixed paths), and business-logic privilege escalation (calling a function that promotes a user's own account tier). Detection requires capturing all URLs visible in admin sessions and replaying each with a low-privilege token.
words.connector: BFLA is like a bank where the vault door has a "manager only" sign but no actual lock — any teller who walks up and turns the handle gets in, because the sign was the only control.
words.techContext: A BFLA finding is confirmed by capturing an admin request such as `DELETE /api/v1/admin/users/42` in Burp Suite, replacing the admin's Bearer token with a regular user's token, replaying the request, and receiving a 200 response instead of 403.
words.exampleSentence: Testers discovered BFLA in the SaaS platform by directly calling the admin user-deletion endpoint with a free-tier account token, successfully removing accounts belonging to paying customers.
words.etymology: OWASP API Security Top 10 term introduced in 2019, distinct from BOLA to separate the data-object access failure (BOLA) from the privileged-function access failure (BFLA); became OWASP API5:2023.

words.shortDefinition: SQL feature that sends query structure and data separately, making structural injection impossible.
words.simpleDefinition: A prepared statement separates the SQL skeleton from the data that fills it. The database compiles the query structure first, then binds the user-supplied values as pure data — not as SQL text. No matter what characters the user supplies, they can never alter the query's structure because the parser has already run.
words.longDefinition: Prepared statements (also called parameterized queries) are the primary and most reliable defense against SQL injection. In the classic vulnerable pattern, user input is concatenated into a query string and the database engine parses the combined result, making it impossible to distinguish developer-intended SQL from attacker-injected SQL. Prepared statements break this by splitting the process into two phases: first, the driver sends the query template with placeholders to the database, which compiles it into an execution plan; second, user-supplied values are bound to those placeholders as typed data parameters. The database engine never re-parses the query with the data values substituted — it executes the pre-compiled plan with the data applied. This structural separation makes SQL injection mechanically impossible for the parameterized portions. Prepared statements work across all major databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, MSSQL, Oracle) and are available in every ORM and database driver. ORMs like SQLAlchemy, Hibernate, and ActiveRecord use prepared statements by default. The only remaining injection surface is dynamically constructed table names or column names — those must be validated against an allowlist because parameters cannot be used for identifiers.
words.connector: A prepared statement is like a form with blank fields: the form's structure is printed in advance and the data is filled in at submission time. An attacker who fills in `Robert'); DROP TABLE students;--` just gets that string stored as a name — the semicolons and SQL keywords are treated as text, not commands.
words.techContext: After switching from string-formatted queries to SQLAlchemy's parameterized syntax, the security team's SQLMap scan returned zero injection findings across 200 endpoints that had previously shown exploitable vulnerabilities.
words.exampleSentence: Migrating 400 raw SQL queries to prepared statements across the legacy PHP codebase eliminated every SQL injection finding in the next penetration test.

codeExample.code:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("app.db")

# VULNERABLE — string concatenation
user_id = request.args["id"]
conn.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + user_id)

# SECURE — prepared statement (parameterized query)
# The ? placeholder is compiled first; user_id is bound as data
conn.execute(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?",
    (user_id,)          # tuple of parameters — never interpreted as SQL
)

words.etymology: "Prepared" refers to the pre-compilation step; the feature dates to the ANSI SQL standard and has been available in most relational database systems since the 1990s; the security framing became prominent with OWASP guidance in the mid-2000s.

words.shortDefinition: Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data; cipher mode providing both confidentiality and integrity in one operation.
words.simpleDefinition: AEAD encrypts data and produces a tamper-detecting authentication tag in a single pass. If anyone modifies the ciphertext or the unencrypted header data (the "associated data") attached to it, decryption fails loudly before any plaintext is released. AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are the two AEAD algorithms developers need to know.
words.longDefinition: Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) solves the failure mode of encryption-only schemes: pure encryption provides confidentiality but not integrity. An attacker can flip bits in a CBC ciphertext and predictably corrupt the decrypted output without knowing the key — a property exploited by padding-oracle attacks. AEAD bakes authentication into the cipher mode. It takes a key, nonce, optional associated data (plaintext metadata), and plaintext, and produces ciphertext plus an authentication tag. Decryption requires the same key, the same nonce, and the same associated data; if any input differs, decryption returns an error before producing any plaintext. The associated data component — authenticated but not encrypted — allows binding unencrypted context (user IDs, protocol version bytes, session metadata) to a ciphertext, preventing context-confusion attacks where a ciphertext encrypted for one context is replayed in another. The two AEAD constructions relevant to developers are AES-GCM (hardware-accelerated on x86/ARM via AES-NI, nonce must be unique per (key, message) pair) and ChaCha20-Poly1305 (software-efficient, resistant to timing side-channels without hardware support, preferred on constrained devices). Both are mandatory in TLS 1.3, which removed all non-AEAD cipher suites.
words.connector: AEAD is like a tamper-evident envelope with a wax seal over both the contents and the recipient's address — if anyone opens the envelope, changes a word, or readdresses it to the wrong person, the seal breaks visibly before the recipient reads it.
words.techContext: When using AES-GCM, generating a fresh cryptographically random 96-bit nonce for every encryption call is mandatory; nonce reuse with the same key is catastrophic and allows recovery of both plaintexts and the authentication key.
words.exampleSentence: Upgrading from AES-CBC to AES-256-GCM eliminated the padding oracle risk and added integrity protection, allowing the API to detect any in-transit modification of encrypted payloads.

codeExample.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
import os

key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)
aesgcm = AESGCM(key)

# Encrypt — nonce must be unique per message
nonce = os.urandom(12)         # 96-bit random nonce
aad   = b"user_id:42"          # associated data — authenticated, not encrypted
ct    = aesgcm.encrypt(nonce, b"secret payload", aad)

# Decrypt — fails with InvalidTag if ciphertext or aad was modified
plaintext = aesgcm.decrypt(nonce, ct, aad)

words.etymology: AEAD is an acronym coined in academic cryptography literature in the early 2000s; the most influential paper is "Authenticated-Encryption with Associated-Data" by Phillip Rogaway (2002), which systematized the concept.

words.shortDefinition: Hash-based Message Authentication Code; keyed hash proving both data integrity and sender authenticity.
words.simpleDefinition: HMAC ties a secret key to a hash function so only someone holding the key can produce or verify the result. It proves two things: the message has not been modified, and it came from a party that knows the shared secret. HMAC-SHA256 is how GitHub signs webhook payloads, how Stripe verifies payment notifications, and how JWTs with shared secrets are authenticated.
words.longDefinition: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) addresses the fundamental limitation of plain hash functions: anyone can compute SHA256(message) without a key, so a plain hash provides no authentication — only integrity. The naive fix of prepending a key (`SHA256(key || message)`) is vulnerable to length extension attacks exploiting the Merkle-Damgard construction of SHA-2, where an attacker knowing the MAC can extend the message and compute a valid MAC for the extended version without knowing the key. HMAC closes this by using a double-hash construction: `HMAC(K, m) = H((K XOR opad) || H((K XOR ipad) || m))`. The inner hash covers the key-padded message; the outer hash covers the key-padded inner result. This structure prevents length extension attacks. HMAC-SHA256 appears throughout production systems: TLS 1.2 PRF uses HMAC-SHA256 to derive keying material; JWT HS256 tokens are HMAC-SHA256 signed; AWS Signature Version 4 signs API requests with a chain of HMAC-SHA256 operations; GitHub, Stripe, and Twilio sign all webhook events with HMAC-SHA256 over the payload. The critical implementation rule: always use constant-time comparison when verifying HMACs, because standard string equality short-circuits on the first differing byte and leaks timing information that allows MAC forgery byte by byte.
words.connector: HMAC is like a wax seal stamped with a unique signet ring — you can verify the seal belongs to the expected sender without being able to forge a matching seal yourself, because you need the ring (the key) to produce it.
words.techContext: When verifying a GitHub webhook signature, compute `HMAC-SHA256(secret, payload)` and compare it to the `X-Hub-Signature-256` header using a constant-time comparison function to prevent timing-based forgery.
words.exampleSentence: The payment service verifies every incoming webhook with HMAC-SHA256 before processing it, ensuring that only Stripe — which holds the shared secret — could have generated the payload.

codeExample.code:
import hmac, hashlib

SECRET = b"super-secret-webhook-key"

def verify_github_webhook(payload: bytes, signature_header: str) -> bool:
    expected = hmac.new(SECRET, payload, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    received = signature_header.removeprefix("sha256=")
    # MUST use constant-time comparison to prevent timing oracle
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, received)

words.etymology: HMAC was defined by Bellare, Canetti, and Krawczyk in RFC 2104 (1997) after the length-extension vulnerability of naive keyed hashing was demonstrated; the acronym stands for Hash-based (or Keyed-Hash) Message Authentication Code.

words.shortDefinition: Key Derivation Function; derives cryptographic keys from passwords or secrets with configurable work cost.
words.simpleDefinition: A KDF is a deliberately slow hash designed to make brute-force attacks expensive. SHA-256 runs billions of times per second on a GPU — useless for passwords. A KDF like Argon2id requires significant RAM and CPU time per computation, turning a GPU cluster into a minor inconvenience. Always use a KDF for password storage, never a plain hash.
words.longDefinition: Key Derivation Functions solve the speed problem of general-purpose hash functions for password storage and key derivation. SHA-256 executes at roughly 10 billion operations per second on modern GPU hardware, meaning an attacker with a leaked password hash database can brute-force typical user passwords in minutes. KDFs address this by being deliberately expensive — tunable to require a fixed amount of CPU time, memory, or both, regardless of how fast the hardware becomes. The three KDFs developers must know are: PBKDF2, which iterates HMAC-SHA256 hundreds of thousands of times (CPU-bound, not memory-hard — GPU attacks remain practical at high iteration counts; use when FIPS compliance is mandatory); scrypt, which adds memory-hardness on top of PBKDF2, requiring a tunable amount of RAM that makes GPU parallelism expensive; and Argon2id, which won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition and is the current consensus recommendation from OWASP, Aumasson's Serious Cryptography, and the real-world-cryptography community. Argon2id requires both memory (m parameter) and time (t parameter), making it simultaneously resistant to GPU attacks and side-channel timing attacks. Every password must be hashed with a unique, cryptographically random salt (16+ bytes) to prevent rainbow table attacks. OWASP's 2024 recommended Argon2id parameters: m=19456 (19 MiB), t=2, p=1.
words.connector: A KDF is a speed bump deliberately engineered into the hashing road — not a yield sign, but a series of deep concrete ridges that force every vehicle to slow down, making the road useless as a drag-racing strip no matter how powerful the engine.
words.techContext: When a password database is leaked, Argon2id-hashed passwords with current parameters require roughly 3 seconds of work per guess on dedicated hardware, compared to milliseconds for SHA-256 — effectively making offline brute-force infeasible for non-trivial passwords.
words.exampleSentence: Replacing the legacy MD5 password hashes with Argon2id reduced the credential-stuffing success rate in penetration tests from 60% to effectively zero against the same wordlist.

codeExample.code:
import argon2  # pip install argon2-cffi

# Argon2id — OWASP 2024 parameters
ph = argon2.PasswordHasher(
    time_cost=2,           # t=2 iterations
    memory_cost=19456,     # m=19 MiB
    parallelism=1,         # p=1
    hash_len=32,
    salt_len=16,
)

hashed = ph.hash("user_password")

try:
    ph.verify(hashed, "user_password")  # True
    if ph.check_needs_rehash(hashed):
        hashed = ph.hash("user_password")  # upgrade on login
except argon2.exceptions.VerifyMismatchError:
    pass  # wrong password

words.etymology: Key Derivation Function is a term from cryptographic standards literature; Argon2 (from Greek argon, 'lazy/slow', evoking the noble-gas inertness) was designed by Biryukov, Dinu, and Großschädl and won the PHC in 2015.

words.shortDefinition: TLS version that removes weak cipher suites, mandates forward secrecy, and reduces handshake round trips.
words.simpleDefinition: TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, 2018) is a near-complete redesign of TLS that strips out every cipher suite and key exchange mechanism behind past attacks — RSA static key exchange, CBC modes, SHA-1, compression — and cuts the connection handshake from two round trips to one. Every remaining cipher suite is AEAD, and forward secrecy is mandatory.
words.longDefinition: TLS 1.3 was standardized in RFC 8446 (August 2018) after four years of development and eliminates the mechanisms behind BEAST, POODLE, DROWN, LOGJAM, FREAK, and the CRIME compression attack in a single stroke. Key changes from TLS 1.2: RSA static key exchange is removed entirely — TLS 1.3 mandates ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange (ECDHE over X25519 or P-256), which provides forward secrecy for every session; all CBC cipher suites are removed, leaving only three AEAD suites (AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305); SHA-1 and MD5 are removed from signature schemes; TLS compression is removed; and session resumption via Diffie-Hellman replaces the insecure session ticket mechanism. The handshake reduces from two round trips to one — the client sends its key share in the first message, and the server responds with its key share and immediately encrypts subsequent messages, making more of the handshake opaque to passive observers. The 0-RTT (zero round-trip) resumption mode allows sending application data in the very first packet when resuming an existing session, but at the cost of replay vulnerability — use only for idempotent, replay-safe operations. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are formally deprecated by RFC 8996 (2021) and prohibited by PCI DSS.
words.connector: TLS 1.3 is the security equivalent of a building evacuation after discovering the old wiring is a fire hazard — rather than patching individual circuits, the entire electrical system was rewired from scratch, and anything that couldn't meet the new code was simply removed.
words.techContext: Configuring an Nginx server for TLS 1.3: set `ssl_protocols TLSv1.3;` and `ssl_prefer_server_ciphers off;` — the latter is correct for 1.3 because all remaining cipher suites are equally strong and client preference can safely be honored.
words.exampleSentence: After enforcing TLS 1.3 minimum on the API gateway, the security scanner's protocol downgrade tests returned zero findings, confirming that all POODLE-era vulnerabilities were no longer reachable.
words.etymology: TLS (Transport Layer Security) replaced SSL in RFC 2246 (1999); version 1.3 designates the fourth major revision, standardized in RFC 8446 (2018) after version 1.2 (RFC 5246, 2008).

words.shortDefinition: Public append-only logs of every TLS certificate issued, enabling detection of misissued or rogue certificates.
words.simpleDefinition: Certificate Transparency requires every TLS certificate issuer (CA) to record certificates in public append-only logs before browsers trust them. Anyone can search these logs for their domains. If an attacker or a compromised CA issues a fraudulent certificate for your domain, you see it in the logs within hours — before it can be used in an undetected man-in-the-middle attack.
words.longDefinition: Certificate Transparency (CT, RFC 6962) was proposed by Ben Laurie at Google in 2013 following the DigiNotar incident — a compromised Dutch CA that issued fraudulent certificates for google.com, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks on Iranian users that went undetected until the certificates appeared in the wild. CT solves the detection problem by requiring CAs to submit every issued certificate to at least two independent, public, append-only CT logs before the certificate becomes trusted. Logs are cryptographically verified Merkle trees: certificates cannot be removed or silently altered. Upon submission, the log returns a Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT) — a cryptographic promise that the certificate was logged — which the CA embeds in the certificate or delivers via TLS extension stapling. Browsers (Chrome since 2018, Safari since 2021) refuse to trust certificates lacking valid SCTs. This means every publicly trusted TLS certificate is visible to domain operators and security researchers. Developers and operators should monitor CT logs for their domains using crt.sh, Cloudflare's CT Monitor, or Facebook's Certificate Transparency Monitoring — receiving alerts when any CA issues any certificate for their domain, which exposes misissued or unauthorized certificates within minutes of issuance.
words.connector: Certificate Transparency is a public noticeboard that every locksmith (CA) must post on before handing out a key copy for your address — you and anyone else can check whether an unauthorized locksmith has recently made a copy without your knowledge.
words.techContext: Searching crt.sh for `%.example.com` reveals every certificate ever issued for that domain and all its subdomains, including wildcard certificates that might have been issued without the domain owner's knowledge.
words.exampleSentence: The security team discovered a rogue wildcard certificate for their domain through CT log monitoring within 90 minutes of a phishing-campaign CA compromise, before any user was targeted.

codeExample.code:
# Query crt.sh for all certificates issued for a domain
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json" \
  | jq '.[] | {id: .id, common_name: .common_name,
               issuer: .issuer_name, logged_at: .entry_timestamp}'

# Monitor for new certificates (run in CI or as a cron job)
# Alert if any unexpected issuers appear in results

words.etymology: "Certificate Transparency" coined by Ben Laurie (Google) in the 2013 RFC 6962 draft; the Merkle tree audit log design draws on transparency concepts from cryptographic verifiable-log literature.

words.shortDefinition: Static Application Security Testing; analyzes source code without executing it to find coding flaws and insecure APIs.
words.simpleDefinition: SAST tools read your source code (or compiled bytecode) looking for patterns that indicate security vulnerabilities — unsanitized data flowing to a SQL sink, calls to dangerous shell APIs, hardcoded credentials. They run before the application is deployed, typically on every commit or pull request, providing fast feedback. The trade-off: high false-positive rates require triage.
words.longDefinition: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) analyzes source code, bytecode, or binary representations without executing the application. The primary technique is taint analysis: tracking data from untrusted sources (HTTP request parameters, headers, file reads) through the codebase to dangerous sinks (SQL queries, shell commands, template renderers, HTML output points). If a data flow path from source to sink lacks appropriate sanitization or parameterization, SAST flags it. Three analysis techniques underpin most SAST tools: pattern or AST matching (simple, fast, high false-positive rate — the tool searches the parsed abstract syntax tree for known-dangerous API calls regardless of reachability); data-flow analysis (more precise — tracks values across variable assignments and function boundaries); and taint analysis (most precise — propagates taint labels through the data-flow graph). Major SAST tools include Semgrep (rule-based, highly customizable, widely used for PR gates), SonarQube/SonarCloud (multi-language, broadly deployed), Checkmarx, Veracode, and CodeQL (GitHub's semantic code analysis engine). SAST's primary limitation is false positives — rates of 10–50% are common — because static analysis cannot model all runtime behavior: a data-flow path may be theoretically vulnerable but unreachable due to runtime access controls. Mature SAST programs use suppression annotations and custom rule tuning to reduce noise.
words.connector: SAST is like a grammar checker for security: it reads your code looking for dangerous sentence structures before you run it, highlighting patterns it knows tend to cause problems — but it sometimes flags valid sentences as suspicious because it lacks the full context of what your program actually does at runtime.
words.techContext: Running Semgrep with the OWASP Top 10 ruleset on every PR provides sub-minute security feedback and can be tuned to block merges only on high-confidence findings, reducing friction while maintaining coverage.
words.exampleSentence: SAST surfaced 14 SQL injection sinks in the legacy PHP module during the first scan, all resulting from string-concatenated queries that had never been reviewed by the security team.

codeExample.code:
# GitHub Actions: run Semgrep SAST on every PR
jobs:
  sast:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run Semgrep
        uses: returntocorp/semgrep-action@v1
        with:
          config: >
            p/owasp-top-ten
            p/python
            p/secrets
        env:
          SEMGREP_APP_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SEMGREP_APP_TOKEN }}

words.etymology: SAST as an acronym was standardized by Gartner in the early 2010s to categorize the static analysis tool market; "static" distinguishes it from dynamic (DAST) and interactive (IAST) testing techniques.

words.shortDefinition: Dynamic Application Security Testing; probes a running application from the outside to find runtime vulnerabilities.
words.simpleDefinition: DAST tools attack your running application from the outside, the way a real attacker would — fuzzing endpoints, testing authentication flows, checking security headers, probing for injection. They require a deployed environment but find vulnerabilities that code analysis misses: misconfigured middleware, unexpected interactions between components, and runtime authentication failures.
words.longDefinition: Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) tests a running application from the outside, mimicking an external attacker's perspective. Unlike SAST, which reads code without running it, DAST exercises the actual running system — HTTP endpoints, authentication flows, session management, input validation — and reports on observable behavior. DAST strengths: low false-positive rates (if the tool confirms an injection by extracting data, the finding is real), discovery of runtime misconfigurations (missing security headers, permissive CORS policies, insecure TLS settings), authentication and session vulnerabilities (session fixation, JWT algorithm confusion), and integration-layer vulnerabilities that are invisible at the code level. DAST limitations: requires a stable deployed environment (typically staging), cannot find vulnerabilities in code paths that are not reachable via HTTP, and may miss business-logic vulnerabilities that require application-specific context. Major DAST tools include OWASP ZAP (open-source, widely used in CI), Burp Suite Pro (manual + automated), Nikto, and commercial platforms like HCL AppScan. In CI/CD pipelines, DAST typically runs against an ephemeral staging environment as a post-deployment gate before promotion to production. The combination of SAST at commit time and DAST at staging provides complementary coverage — SAST finds what code looks dangerous, DAST finds what the running system actually does.
words.connector: DAST is a burglar who tries every window and door on your house while you're in it — not reading the blueprints, but actually testing whether each lock holds under pressure, discovering that the back door was left unlocked despite the blueprint showing it secured.
words.techContext: Integrating OWASP ZAP's baseline scan into a CI pipeline with `zap-baseline.py -t https://staging.example.com` provides automated discovery of common misconfigurations and injection points with no manual configuration.
words.exampleSentence: DAST against the staging environment revealed a reflected XSS in the error message path that SAST had missed because the vulnerability arose from a third-party template library, not first-party code.

# GitHub Actions: OWASP ZAP DAST baseline scan
jobs:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: deploy-staging
    steps:
      - name: ZAP Baseline Scan
        uses: zaproxy/action-baseline@v0.10.0
        with:
          target: 'https://staging.example.com'

words.etymology: DAST is a Gartner-coined acronym from the early 2010s, distinguishing tools that test running applications (dynamic) from those that analyze code statically (SAST); the category encompasses web application scanning and API fuzzing.

words.shortDefinition: Software Composition Analysis; inventories open-source dependencies and checks them against known CVE databases.
words.simpleDefinition: SCA tools scan your project's dependency tree — direct and transitive dependencies — and cross-reference every package version against vulnerability databases like the NVD and GitHub Advisory Database. When Log4Shell or OpenSSL vulnerabilities drop, SCA tells you within minutes which of your services are affected and which versions to upgrade to.
words.longDefinition: Software Composition Analysis (SCA) addresses the reality that modern applications are composed mostly of third-party open-source libraries. In a typical Node.js or Python application, first-party code may represent less than 10% of total executable lines; the rest is dependencies. SCA tools generate a dependency inventory (equivalent to an SBOM) and check every package against CVE databases including the National Vulnerability Database (NVD), GitHub Advisory Database, Snyk Vulnerability DB, and OSV.dev. SCA runs at build time or on every dependency installation and provides immediate feedback on vulnerable packages, along with remediation guidance (safe upgrade versions or mitigations). Beyond CVE matching, advanced SCA tools perform reachability analysis — determining whether the vulnerable function in a dependency is actually called by the application code, dramatically reducing false positives. SCA also covers license compliance, flagging copyleft licenses (GPL, AGPL) that may impose obligations in commercial software. Leading SCA tools include Snyk Open Source, Dependabot (GitHub-native, free), OWASP Dependency-Check, Mend.io (formerly WhiteSource), and Trivy (container + dependency scanning). The 2021 Log4Shell vulnerability demonstrated SCA's value: organizations with mature SCA programs identified all affected services within hours; those without took weeks of manual auditing.
words.connector: SCA is like a food recall notification system for code — when a supplier announces that a specific batch of an ingredient is contaminated, your inventory system automatically flags every dish that used that batch, so you know exactly what to pull from the menu.
words.techContext: Running `snyk test` as a CI gate with `--severity-threshold=high` blocks merges when any direct or transitive dependency contains a known high- or critical-severity CVE, while `--fail-on=upgradable` limits noise to only actionable findings.
words.exampleSentence: The SCA scan flagged a transitive dependency on Log4j 2.14.1 in three services within minutes of CVE-2021-44228 publication, enabling the team to patch before any public exploit code was circulated.

words.shortDefinition: Interactive Application Security Testing; instruments the running app internally while tests exercise it.
words.simpleDefinition: IAST instruments the application from the inside — adding sensors to the runtime that observe data flows as automated tests or real traffic exercises the application. Because IAST sees actual tainted data moving through actual code paths, it has very low false-positive rates and finds vulnerabilities that neither SAST nor DAST can detect in isolation.
words.longDefinition: Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST) embeds a security sensor — typically a Java agent, .NET profiler, or instrumented runtime — directly into the running application. As automated tests, DAST scans, or real traffic exercise the application, the IAST agent monitors data flows in real time: it tracks whether HTTP request parameters flow into SQL queries without parameterization, whether deserialized objects from the network reach dangerous methods, whether cryptographic APIs are called with insecure parameters. Because IAST observes actual execution of actual code with actual data, it achieves near-zero false-positive rates for the code paths that are exercised — it is not guessing about what might happen statically, it is reporting what did happen dynamically. IAST's principal limitation is coverage: vulnerabilities in code paths not exercised during the test session remain invisible. The technique is most effective when combined with high-coverage automated integration test suites that exercise the application's full API surface. IAST differs from RASP (Runtime Application Self-Protection) in intent: IAST is a testing-time diagnostic tool that reports findings to developers; RASP is a production-time defense that blocks attacks in real time. Tools include Contrast Security (the category creator), Seeker (Synopsys), HCL AppScan, and Checkmarx IAST.
words.connector: IAST is like a doctor who instruments a patient with wireless biosensors and then has them run on a treadmill — instead of guessing from a static scan what might happen under exertion, it observes the actual heart rate, oxygen, and blood pressure in real time as stress is applied.
words.techContext: Deploying a Contrast IAST agent to the integration test environment and running the full API test suite provides near-zero false-positive taint-analysis results without modifying application code, surfacing vulnerabilities that SAST's static analysis missed.
words.exampleSentence: IAST discovered a second-order SQL injection vulnerability that SAST missed entirely because the tainted data was stored in the database during one request and used in a query during a completely different request two test steps later.
